Chapter 9: Ethical Influence—Using the Principles for Good.
Let’s get real for a second—these principles of influence? They aren’t good or bad on their own. They’re tools. And just like any tool, it all comes down to how you use them.
In your everyday life—whether you’re at work, at home, or out in your community—understanding these levers can actually help you build real trust, spark cooperation, and create positive change.
Think about this: If you’re a leader, you might use social proof to shine a light on the great work your team’s doing, nudging others to step up too. Or, if you’re a teacher, you could tap into commitment and consistency by having your students set learning goals and share them out loud. Even a nonprofit can use reciprocity, offering up valuable information for free before ever asking for support.
The thread running through all of this? Ethical influence. That means you’re guided by transparency, respect, and a real desire to help—not by hidden motives or heavy-handed tactics. No one wants to feel like they’re being tricked or pressured, right?
So, here are three quick questions to keep you on track:
First, am I trying to help—or just to get something out of this?
Second, am I being totally honest about why I’m asking?
And finally, would I feel good about this if the roles were flipped?
When you hold yourself—and your influence—to these standards, you turn it into a real force for good. It deepens relationships, brings communities closer, and helps everyone work toward goals they actually care about.
